questions.question: What is the main developmental problem after neurons have been generated, differentiated, migrated, and selected for survival?
options: Connecting them into functional circuits
Returning them to proliferative zones
Converting them into neural crest cells
Eliminating all remaining axons
questions.feedback: The next developmental problem is to connect neurons into functional circuits.

questions.question: Which three major phases organize neural-circuit development in the lesson?
options: Axon growth and guidance, synaptogenesis, and myelination
Neurogenesis, migration, and apoptosis
Differentiation, pruning, and necrosis
Proliferation, migration, and myelination
questions.feedback: The lesson organizes circuit formation into axon growth and guidance, synaptogenesis, and myelination.

questions.question: What is the growth cone?
options: A dynamic structure at the tip of a growing axon
A postsynaptic receptor cluster
A glial cell that produces myelin
A region of the muscle basal lamina
questions.feedback: The growth cone is the highly dynamic structure at the tip of a growing axon.

questions.question: What is the main role of filopodia in the growth cone?
options: Exploring the surrounding environment
Producing neurotransmitter
Forming compact myelin
Breaking down acetylcholine
questions.feedback: Filopodia extend from the growth cone and explore the surrounding environment.

questions.question: What is the main role of lamellipodia in the growth cone?
options: They extend and retract during growth
They form nodes of Ranvier
They synthesize myelin proteins
They cluster acetylcholine receptors
questions.feedback: Lamellipodia are dynamic growth-cone structures that extend and retract.

questions.question: How are guidance signals translated into changes in axonal direction?
options: Through cytoskeletal changes in the growth cone
By changing the neuronal genome
By eliminating the nucleus
By producing myelin around the growth cone
questions.feedback: Signals detected by the growth cone are translated into cytoskeletal changes that determine axonal direction.

questions.question: Why is axon guidance described as a stepwise process?
options: Axons encounter intermediate cues and choice points along their route
Axons stop growing after every cell division
The final target continuously moves
Guidance occurs only after synaptogenesis
questions.feedback: Axons make a sequence of local decisions at intermediate cues and choice points.

questions.question: Which statement best summarizes long-range axon guidance?
options: Repeated local decisions can produce the correct long-range connection
One single cue determines the complete route
Axons connect randomly and are organized only later
Growth cones do not respond to extracellular signals
questions.feedback: The lesson summarizes long-range guidance as a sequence of local decisions.

questions.question: What role does laminin play in axon guidance?
options: It can provide a permissive extracellular-matrix substrate
It blocks all growth-cone adhesion
It is a voltage-gated sodium channel
It causes synaptic vesicle release
questions.feedback: Laminin can provide a permissive substrate on which growth cones attach and extend.

questions.question: What role does NCAM play during axon growth?
options: It promotes adhesion between neural cells
It breaks down acetylcholine
It acts as a myelin lipid
It is a diffusible chemorepellent
questions.feedback: NCAM is a cell-adhesion molecule that promotes interactions between neural cells.

questions.question: What is fasciculation?
options: The growth of axons along other axons
The elimination of dendrites
The formation of postsynaptic receptor clusters
The production of extracellular matrix by muscle
questions.feedback: Fasciculation is the process by which growing axons adhere to and follow pre-existing axons.

questions.question: What is the role of pioneer axons?
options: They establish an initial route that later axons can follow
They form the first oligodendrocytes
They prevent all later axon growth
They generate the synaptic basal lamina
questions.feedback: Pioneer axons can establish an initial path used by later-growing axons.

questions.question: Which molecule is used in the lesson as an example of chemoattraction?
options: Netrin
Agrin
PSD-95
Caspr
questions.feedback: Netrin is used as an example of a diffusible cue that can attract a growth cone.

questions.question: Which molecule is used as an example of contact-mediated repulsion?
options: Ephrins
AChE
Neuroligin
Rapsyn
questions.feedback: Ephrins can produce contact-mediated growth-cone collapse or redirection.

questions.question: Can netrin act as both an attractive and a repulsive cue?
options: Yes, depending on the competence of the growth cone
No, it is always attractive
No, it acts only as an adhesion molecule
Only after myelination
questions.feedback: The lesson emphasizes that netrin can attract or repel depending on the responding growth cone.

questions.question: What determines the final direction of growth-cone movement?
options: Integration of multiple local signals
A single universal guidance molecule
Only axon diameter
Only the position of the nucleus
questions.feedback: Growth direction reflects the combined effect of multiple local signals.

questions.question: What did Sperry's chemoaffinity hypothesis propose?
options: Neurons and targets carry molecular information that helps specify appropriate connections
Axons connect randomly to the nearest target
Synapses form only after myelination
Circuit specificity is generated exclusively by activity
questions.feedback: Sperry proposed matching molecular information between projecting neurons and their targets.

questions.question: In Sperry's eye-rotation experiment, what happened after the optic nerve was cut?
options: Retinal axons were allowed to regenerate
The eye was permanently removed
The tectum was replaced by muscle
All retinal neurons immediately died
questions.feedback: The frog eye was rotated, the optic nerve was cut, and retinal axons were allowed to regenerate.

questions.question: What was observed after retinal axons regenerated in Sperry's experiment?
options: They returned approximately to their original tectal locations
They connected randomly across the tectum
They failed to enter the brain
They projected only to the ipsilateral side
questions.feedback: Regenerating retinal axons tended to return to their previous topographic positions.

questions.question: Why was visually guided behavior inappropriate after regeneration in Sperry's experiment?
options: The eye remained rotated while axons re-established their original tectal map
The retina had no photoreceptors
The optic nerve regenerated to the spinal cord
The tectum no longer contained neurons
questions.feedback: The original mapping was restored despite the 180-degree rotation of the eye.

questions.question: What is a topographic map?
options: An ordered projection that preserves spatial relationships between neighboring neurons
A random arrangement of synapses
A map of only glial cells
A list of neurotransmitters in a circuit in the context of normal nervous-system development
questions.feedback: Topographic maps preserve spatial relationships between neighboring cells in a projection.

questions.question: What is a retinotopic map?
options: An ordered representation of retinal spatial organization in a central target
A map of muscle fibers in the spinal cord during the establishment of stable neural connections
A map of oligodendrocytes in white matter
A pattern of neurotransmitter release at the NMJ
questions.feedback: A retinotopic map preserves the spatial organization of the retina in a central target.

questions.question: How can topographic maps be generated without a unique molecular label for every neuron?
options: Using graded molecular signals
Using only electrical synapses throughout the maturation of the circuit
Using random branching
Using apoptosis alone
questions.feedback: Molecular gradients can provide continuous positional information.

questions.question: What is the role of Eph receptors and ephrins in the lesson?
options: They help guide the formation of topographic projections
They directly form synaptic vesicles at this stage of neural development
They produce myelin
They break down acetylcholine
questions.feedback: Graded Eph/ephrin expression contributes to ordered topographic projections.

questions.question: For some retinal axons, what effect does increasing ephrin concentration have?
options: It acts as a repulsive signal
It always causes synapse formation in the context of normal nervous-system development
It stimulates myelin production
It removes all Eph receptors
questions.feedback: Increasing ephrin concentration can act as a repulsive cue for some retinal axons.

questions.question: Which of the following is a contact-dependent guidance mechanism?
options: Fasciculation
Chemoattraction
Chemorepulsion by a diffusible cue
Long-range diffusion of netrin
questions.feedback: Fasciculation is a contact-dependent guidance mechanism.

questions.question: Which of the following is a diffusible guidance mechanism?
options: Chemoattraction
Fasciculation
Cell-surface adhesion
Extracellular-matrix adhesion
questions.feedback: Chemoattraction and chemorepulsion are diffusible guidance mechanisms.

questions.question: Why does adhesion influence growth-cone movement beyond simply attaching the axon?
options: It can activate intracellular signaling pathways
It changes the axon's DNA sequence
It directly produces myelin
It removes all actin from the growth cone
questions.feedback: Adhesive interactions can trigger intracellular pathways that influence growth-cone movement.

questions.question: What is a developmental choice point?
options: A region where a growing axon must make a directional decision
A stage where all synapses are eliminated during the refinement of developing neural pathways
A point where myelin is synthesized
A location where neurons divide symmetrically
questions.feedback: Choice points are intermediate regions where axons select between alternative routes.

questions.question: What developmental decision is illustrated by the optic chiasm?
options: Whether retinal axons cross the midline or remain ipsilateral
Whether muscle fibers receive myelin
Whether neurons undergo apoptosis
Whether synapses use acetylcholine or glutamate throughout the maturation of the circuit
questions.feedback: At the optic chiasm, retinal axons may cross or remain ipsilateral.

questions.question: Why can an intermediate target be important even if it is not the final destination?
options: It can act as a navigation checkpoint
It permanently stops axon growth
It causes all axons to become glia throughout the maturation of the circuit
It removes all guidance receptors
questions.feedback: Intermediate targets can act as navigation checkpoints during long-range growth.

questions.question: What does axonal competence mean in the context of guidance?
options: The ability of the growth cone to interpret a guidance signal
The speed of synaptic transmission
The number of muscle fibers in a motor unit during the establishment of stable neural connections
The amount of myelin around an axon
questions.feedback: Axonal competence is the state that determines how a growth cone interprets a cue.

questions.question: Which factor can influence how a growth cone responds to a guidance cue?
options: Which receptors are expressed
Only the age of the organism
Only target-cell diameter
Only the presence of myelin
questions.feedback: Receptor expression, receptor levels, and intracellular signaling state influence guidance responses.

questions.question: Can the same extracellular cue produce different responses in different axons?
options: Yes, because axons can differ in receptor expression and intracellular state
No, every axon always responds identically as development proceeds toward a mature circuit
Only after synaptogenesis
Only in muscle
questions.feedback: Different axons can interpret the same signal differently because their competence differs.

questions.question: Why is reaching the correct target region not sufficient for circuit formation?
options: The axon must still select the correct cell and often the correct subcellular compartment
Axons cannot form synapses in target regions throughout the maturation of the circuit as development proceeds toward a mature circuit
Only glial cells determine final connectivity
All target cells in one region are identical throughout the maturation of the circuit as development proceeds toward a mature circuit
questions.feedback: Circuit formation requires specificity at the level of target cell and often subcellular compartment.

questions.question: What is synaptogenesis?
options: The process by which neurons establish specialized communication sites with target cells
The formation of the neural tube once the relevant target region has been reached
The elimination of all immature neurons during the establishment of stable neural connections
The wrapping of axons by oligodendrocytes
questions.feedback: Synaptogenesis is the formation of specialized synaptic communication sites.

questions.question: Which event occurs on the presynaptic side during synapse formation?
options: Synaptic vesicles accumulate
Acetylcholine receptors cluster in the muscle membrane
Postsynaptic scaffolds are eliminated
Myelin wraps are compacted
questions.feedback: The presynaptic terminal accumulates vesicles and recruits active-zone and release machinery.

questions.question: Which event occurs on the postsynaptic side during synapse formation?
options: Receptors become concentrated
Synaptic vesicles accumulate in the postsynaptic membrane
The axon initial segment disappears
The basal lamina is removed
questions.feedback: Postsynaptic receptors and scaffolding proteins become concentrated.

questions.question: Why is synapse formation described as a coordinated process?
options: Pre- and postsynaptic specializations develop together through bidirectional signaling
Only the presynaptic neuron changes at this stage of neural development
Only the postsynaptic cell changes as development proceeds toward a mature circuit
Synapses form without cell-cell interaction
questions.feedback: Both sides of the developing synapse undergo coordinated changes.

questions.question: Why has the neuromuscular junction been a useful model for synaptogenesis?
options: It is large, anatomically well defined, and experimentally accessible
It is the smallest synapse in the nervous system during the refinement of developing neural pathways
It contains no extracellular matrix once the relevant target region has been reached
It uses many neurotransmitters simultaneously
questions.feedback: Its accessibility and clear organization make the neuromuscular junction an effective experimental model.

questions.question: What are the three main components of the neuromuscular junction?
options: Presynaptic terminal, synaptic basal lamina, postsynaptic membrane
Axon hillock, node of Ranvier, oligodendrocyte in the context of normal nervous-system development
Dendrite, soma, nucleus
Retina, optic nerve, tectum during the refinement of developing neural pathways
questions.feedback: The NMJ consists of the motor axon terminal, synaptic basal lamina, and postsynaptic muscle membrane.

questions.question: What is the synaptic basal lamina at the neuromuscular junction?
options: A specialized extracellular matrix between nerve and muscle
A layer of myelin around the motor axon during the refinement of developing neural pathways
A cluster of presynaptic vesicles
A region of the muscle nucleus during the establishment of stable neural connections
questions.feedback: The synaptic basal lamina is the specialized extracellular matrix between the nerve terminal and muscle fiber.

questions.question: What did the muscle-regeneration experiment show when nerve regrowth was prevented?
options: The new muscle fiber still formed postsynaptic specializations at the original synaptic site
No muscle regeneration occurred at this stage of neural development in the context of normal nervous-system development
Postsynaptic specializations formed randomly
The basal lamina disappeared immediately in the context of normal nervous-system development once the relevant target region has been reached
questions.feedback: Postsynaptic specializations re-formed at the original synaptic site even without nerve regrowth.

questions.question: What did the nerve-regeneration experiment show?
options: Regenerating motor axons preferentially re-formed terminals at the original synaptic site
Regenerating axons avoided the original synaptic site during the establishment of stable neural connections
Regenerated axons became oligodendrocytes
Only electrical synapses were formed in the context of normal nervous-system development
questions.feedback: Regenerating motor axons preferentially re-formed terminals at the original synaptic site.

questions.question: What conclusion follows from the NMJ regeneration experiments?
options: The synaptic basal lamina contains stable molecular cues that help organize synaptic differentiation
The basal lamina has only a passive structural role during the establishment of stable neural connections
Synaptic location is determined only by activity in the context of normal nervous-system development
Muscle fibers cannot regenerate without nerve contact
questions.feedback: The experiments show that the basal lamina preserves instructive information about synaptic location.

questions.question: Which molecule in the synaptic basal lamina breaks down acetylcholine?
options: Acetylcholinesterase
Agrin during normal circuit development
Neuroligin during the refinement of developing neural pathways
Netrin
questions.feedback: Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) hydrolyzes acetylcholine.

questions.question: Which molecule released by the motor neuron becomes concentrated in the synaptic basal lamina?
options: Agrin
Caspr
PSD-95
Kv1.2
questions.feedback: Agrin is released by the motor neuron and becomes concentrated in the synaptic basal lamina.

questions.question: What receptor does agrin bind on the muscle side?
options: LRP4
Nav once the relevant target region has been reached
NMDAR once the relevant target region has been reached
NCAM
questions.feedback: Agrin binds LRP4, which activates MuSK signaling.

questions.question: What is the main consequence of agrin-LRP4-MuSK signaling?
options: Clustering of acetylcholine receptors
Elimination of all muscle receptors
Formation of myelin
Retraction of all motor axons
questions.feedback: Agrin-LRP4-MuSK signaling promotes ACh receptor clustering through proteins including rapsyn.

questions.question: What is transient polyinnervation?
options: Temporary innervation of one immature muscle fiber by several motor axons
Permanent innervation of one muscle fiber by many motor axons during normal circuit development
Myelination of one axon by several oligodendrocytes during the establishment of stable neural connections
Formation of several nuclei in one neuron during the refinement of developing neural pathways
questions.feedback: During development, immature muscle fibers are initially contacted by several motor axons.

questions.question: What normally happens to transient polyinnervation during maturation?
options: Some inputs are stabilized while others retract, leaving one motor-neuron input per muscle fiber
All motor inputs remain permanently in the context of normal nervous-system development once the relevant target region has been reached
All motor inputs are eliminated during normal circuit development during the refinement of developing neural pathways
The muscle becomes innervated only by sensory neurons at this stage of neural development during the refinement of developing neural pathways
questions.feedback: Competing motor inputs are progressively refined until a single motor-neuron input remains.

questions.question: What happens when ACh receptors are locally blocked at a developing neuromuscular junction?
options: Presynaptic branches withdraw from the blocked region
Presynaptic branches become permanently stabilized during the establishment of stable neural connections
All muscle fibers die immediately once the relevant target region has been reached
Myelination increases locally throughout the maturation of the circuit
questions.feedback: Local ACh receptor blockade causes withdrawal of presynaptic branches from the less active region.

questions.question: What does the ACh-receptor blockade experiment demonstrate?
options: Synaptic refinement is activity-dependent
Synaptic refinement is independent of activity
Only the basal lamina determines branch survival
Motor axons cannot retract during development
questions.feedback: The experiment demonstrates that stabilization and elimination of developing contacts depend on activity.

questions.question: Which of the following is a constructive process in circuit development?
options: Synapse formation
Branch retraction
Synapse elimination
Pruning of inappropriate projections
questions.feedback: Constructive processes include axon extension, branching, dendritic growth, and synapse formation.

questions.question: Which of the following is a regressive process in circuit development?
options: Branch retraction
Axon extension once the relevant target region has been reached
Dendritic growth throughout the maturation of the circuit
Synapse formation once the relevant target region has been reached
questions.feedback: Regressive processes include branch retraction, synapse elimination, and pruning.

questions.question: What general principle is illustrated by activity-dependent synaptic refinement?
options: Overproduction followed by selective stabilization and elimination
Perfect specificity from the first contact at this stage of neural development
Elimination without prior growth throughout the maturation of the circuit
Circuit formation without activity at this stage of neural development
questions.feedback: Mature circuitry emerges through overproduction followed by selective stabilization and elimination.

questions.question: Why were CNS synapses historically difficult to study directly?
options: They are extremely small and near the resolution limit of conventional light microscopy
They exist only during sleep throughout the maturation of the circuit during the refinement of developing neural pathways
They contain no membranes during the establishment of stable neural connections as development proceeds toward a mature circuit
They are larger than entire neurons in the context of normal nervous-system development once the relevant target region has been reached
questions.feedback: CNS synapses are very small and lie close to the resolution limit of light microscopy.

questions.question: What technological development enabled direct structural visualization of CNS synapses?
options: Electron microscopy
Golgi staining alone
PCR
Magnetic stimulation
questions.feedback: Electron microscopy provided direct structural visualization of synaptic ultrastructure.

questions.question: Why is the neuromuscular junction simpler to use as a model than many CNS synapses?
options: CNS synapses are more heterogeneous in transmitter, structure, stability, and can show co-release
CNS synapses are all identical during the establishment of stable neural connections in the context of normal nervous-system development
The NMJ has no receptors during the establishment of stable neural connections once the relevant target region has been reached
The NMJ does not use neurotransmitters during normal circuit development during the establishment of stable neural connections
questions.feedback: CNS synapses are more heterogeneous and can differ in transmitter, structure, stability, and co-release.

questions.question: What does synaptic specificity mean?
options: Neurons form synapses selectively with particular targets and compartments
Neurons connect with any nearby cell equally in the context of normal nervous-system development
All synapses occur on the soma at this stage of neural development
All synapses use the same neurotransmitter in the context of normal nervous-system development
questions.feedback: Synaptic specificity means that neurons select particular targets and often particular subcellular compartments.

questions.question: What is an axosomatic synapse?
options: A synapse onto the cell body
A synapse onto another axon at this stage of neural development
A synapse onto a dendrite once the relevant target region has been reached
A synapse between two muscle fibers during the establishment of stable neural connections
questions.feedback: Axosomatic synapses contact the postsynaptic soma.

questions.question: What is an axodendritic synapse?
options: A synapse onto a dendrite
A synapse onto a muscle fiber
A synapse onto another axon
A synapse between glial cells
questions.feedback: Axodendritic synapses contact a postsynaptic dendrite.

questions.question: What is an axoaxonic synapse?
options: A synapse in which an axon contacts another axon
A synapse in which a dendrite contacts a muscle fiber
A synapse between two dendrites only
A synapse between oligodendrocytes
questions.feedback: Axoaxonic synapses are contacts made onto another axon.

questions.question: Which interneuron class preferentially targets distal dendritic regions?
options: SST interneurons
Chandelier cells only
Motor neurons
Retinal ganglion cells
questions.feedback: The lesson states that SST interneurons preferentially target distal dendritic regions.

questions.question: Which interneuron class often targets the soma and proximal dendrites?
options: PV interneurons
SST interneurons only
Oligodendrocytes
Retinal ganglion cells
questions.feedback: Many PV interneurons preferentially target the soma and proximal dendrites.

questions.question: Which interneuron type selectively innervates the axon initial segment?
options: Chandelier cells
SST interneurons in the context of normal nervous-system development
Astrocytes during the establishment of stable neural connections
Motor neurons during the establishment of stable neural connections
questions.feedback: Chandelier cells selectively target the axon initial segment.

questions.question: What does the Purkinje-cell example illustrate?
options: Neuronal compartments can contain molecular cues that help incoming axons identify the correct synaptic location
All synapses form randomly within a neuron in the context of normal nervous-system development during the establishment of stable neural connections
Only extracellular matrix determines targeting in the context of normal nervous-system development throughout the maturation of the circuit
Subcellular targeting occurs only in muscle during the refinement of developing neural pathways in the context of normal nervous-system development
questions.feedback: The example illustrates molecular specification of a precise subcellular synaptic target.

questions.question: What role do astrocytes play in synaptogenesis?
options: They release signals that promote synapse formation and maturation
They prevent all synapse formation during the establishment of stable neural connections
They function only as passive structural cells throughout the maturation of the circuit
They replace presynaptic neurons throughout the maturation of the circuit
questions.feedback: Astrocytes actively influence synapse formation and maturation.

questions.question: Which astrocyte-derived molecules are mentioned as synaptogenic signals?
options: Thrombospondins
Ephrins
Nav channels
Agrin only
questions.feedback: The lesson mentions thrombospondins as astrocyte-derived synaptogenic signals.

questions.question: What is the role of neurexins and neuroligins during synapse development?
options: They contribute to trans-synaptic adhesion and alignment of pre- and postsynaptic specializations
They form compact myelin throughout the maturation of the circuit as development proceeds toward a mature circuit
They break down neurotransmitters in the context of normal nervous-system development at this stage of neural development
They guide retinal axons to the tectum once the relevant target region has been reached
questions.feedback: Neurexin-neuroligin interactions help stabilize and organize developing synaptic contacts.
